reports.title: From a cortical electrode to a wider BCI platform
reports.scope: Temporary Layer 7-T; original US component market, with wider BCI development treated separately
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

Precision Neuroscience illustrates a staged route from an enabling component to a much wider neurotechnology ambition. Layer 7-T is a temporary cortical electrode cleared in the United States in 2025. A permanent assistive brain–computer interface (BCI) is a different development and commercial proposition. Keeping that boundary clear makes the entrepreneurial case more convincing: early capital and manufacturing capability can support a platform, while each product still needs its own clinical purpose, evidence and payment route. [@FDA-PRECISION-K242618] [@PRECISION-HOME]

The strongest public evidence concerns the electrode's engineering, its clearance, an early financing sequence and a fabrication acquisition. The weakest part is the commercial value of the temporary component in a defined clinical service. No verified price, purchasing contract or product-specific payer policy was identified. Consequently, this report analyses a documented route to market and an incompletely demonstrated adoption case, rather than assuming that better neural recording automatically produces a viable clinical business.

## Device and case boundaries

Layer 7-T places a flexible electrode array against the cortical surface. Its electrodes interface with recording, monitoring and stimulation equipment. The cleared indication permits temporary use for less than 30 days, through open or burr-hole procedures. This gives the report a specific marketed product. Research involving decoding and control of another device provides development context, but does not expand that indication. [@FDA-PRECISION-K242618]

The engineering attraction is a conformable surface interface with many recording sites. In principle, sampling more locations can improve spatial information while avoiding penetration by the recording contacts. The clinical question is more demanding: whether the information changes a surgical or diagnostic decision sufficiently to justify the additional equipment, integration and training. That distinction connects the five sections below.

## 1. Unmet medical need

For the temporary electrode, the unmet need should be defined around obtaining useful cortical information during an appropriate neurosurgical pathway. A general population with paralysis is a poor starting denominator because the cleared component does not itself constitute a permanent assistive BCI. Likewise, the number of people with a neurological diagnosis is not the number who need cortical-surface recording. A defensible market estimate would begin with procedures in which such recording is clinically useful, then apply eligibility, institutional capability and adoption constraints. The reviewed sources do not supply that count. [@FDA-PRECISION-K242618]

The most informative original technical study is Hettick and colleagues' platform report. Its acute human pilot involved five neurosurgical patients: two under general anaesthesia and three during awake language mapping. Together with the engineering experiments, it supports feasibility of placing the interface and obtaining useful signals in a surgical setting. Precision supported the work and numerous authors disclosed company relationships. The small, acute study cannot establish lasting assistive benefit, population-wide effectiveness or lower total care costs. [@PRECISION-HETTICK-2025]

The relevant comparison is therefore an existing cortical-recording workflow, rather than no neurological care. Additional spatial information might support better interpretation, but contact density is an engineering attribute, not a patient outcome. An evaluation would need to measure whether the array changes clinical decisions, whether those changes improve outcomes, and whether setup or interpretation creates extra work. These are analytical requirements, not benefits already demonstrated by the five-patient pilot.

The same discipline applies to costs. No observed before/after cost study for the selected temporary component was verified. The appropriate resource comparison includes the electrode, supporting equipment, operating-room time, staff training and interpretation. A hypothetical saving in surgery time would need evidence of both time released and a financial consequence; shorter time does not automatically reduce a hospital's cash expenditure. The report can explain this value hypothesis, but cannot responsibly quantify savings from the available evidence.

## 2. Intellectual property

A technically close publication is US20230210427A1, *Systems and methods for neural interfaces*. It names Benjamin Rapoport, Demetrios Papageorgiou, Mark Hettick, Adam Poole and Elton Ho, claims priority from 31 December 2021, and records assignment to Precision. This is a published application; the reviewed metadata and text do not constitute a current prosecution or enforceability audit. The inventors' employment at the time of invention was not independently reconstructed. [@PRECISION-ARRAY-IP]

All four independent claims in this publication were read for this draft. Their main content is summarised below; the descriptions are shortened explanations, not legal claim construction.

| Claim | Main content and relevance |
|---|---|
| 1 | A flexible substrate with connected, separable microelectrode-array modules, nonpenetrating contacts and a pocket receiving an insertion paddle. This concerns the physical interface and delivery connection. |
| 5 | Implantation through an approximately tangential cranial opening, with dural access, paddle-guided advancement into the subdural space and withdrawal of the paddle. This concerns the insertion method. |
| 13 | Fabrication of an adhesive-backed polyimide pocket, including laser cutting, folding, alignment and pressure attachment to an array. This concerns a manufacturing method. |
| 17 | Implanting the specified interface, recording and decoding neural signals, and controlling a secondary device. This reaches a BCI use beyond temporary recording alone. |

*Table 1. Independent claims in US20230210427A1. Technical similarity identifies a candidate relationship; it does not prove that every feature is present in the marketed Layer 7-T.* [@PRECISION-ARRAY-IP]

The distinction between claims 1/5 and claim 17 matters commercially. The same invention family can address an interface, its insertion, its manufacture and a future application. A clearance for an electrode does not establish permission for every patented use, and a patent claim does not establish clinical effectiveness. An exact product-to-claim comparison would require the final device drawings and a check of every claim element.

The manufacturing method also suggests why protection may extend beyond a single electrode geometry. Process knowledge, reliable fabrication and integration can affect the difficulty of replication. These are plausible sources of advantage; no undisclosed trade-secret inventory is asserted here. Neither this application nor a portfolio count establishes freedom to operate. The evidence supports an explanation of candidate protection and development strategy, while leaving the complete first-version IP and employment chain incomplete.

## 3. Fundraising

Precision announced a $12 million Series A in May 2021, led by Steadview Capital and B Capital Group's Ascent Team. B Capital subsequently described Precision as a portfolio company and discussed its early development. This gives a responsible-party cross-check of the investor relationship, although the investor article does not independently establish the transaction amount. [@PRECISION-SERIESA-2021] [@PRECISION-BCAPITAL-2021]

The January 2023 company announcement reports a $41 million Series B led by Forepont Capital Partners and $53 million raised in total. The disclosed total is consistent with the two stated rounds. It remains a company-level account, rather than a schedule assigning capital to the temporary array, chronic interface, software or future clinical programmes. No valuation was disclosed in the reviewed records. [@PRECISION-FIN]

| Milestone | Verified financing information | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| May 2021 | $12m Series A | Early platform/company development capital. |
| January 2023 | $41m Series B; $53m cumulative announced | Subsequent development and scale-up capital. |
| October 2023 | Manufacturing acquisition announced; purchase price not verified | A capability milestone, not another quantified funding round. |

*Table 2. Disclosed company financing and a later manufacturing milestone. Dollar amounts are the original announced US-dollar figures; no inflation adjustment or device-budget allocation is implied.* [@PRECISION-SERIESA-2021] [@PRECISION-FIN] [@PRECISION-FACTORY-2023]

The financing sequence supports an entrepreneurial interpretation of staged investment: establish the technology, increase organisational and production capacity, then pursue a defined market entry. It does not establish the investors' actual decision criteria or prove that clearance was funded by a particular fraction of either round. Those would require board, investor or management evidence.

The earliest founders' contributions and a complete first-version development budget remain unknown. A bottom-up reconstruction would sum engineering staff-years, fabrication iterations, verification, sterilisation/packaging validation, regulatory work and clinical evaluation through a specified milestone. A top-down check would use comparable temporary cortical electrodes at the same stage, separating them from permanent BCI programmes. Staff effort and comparable attributable budgets were not verified, so this draft does not manufacture a numerical range. This is a substantive funding limitation despite the useful round history.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

FDA K242618 cleared Layer 7-T on 30 March 2025 as a Class II cortical electrode under 21 CFR 882.1310, product code GYC. The route used substantial equivalence to an existing cortical-electrode predicate. The record supplies a concrete early-market endpoint: temporary recording, monitoring and stimulation with suitable equipment, rather than authorisation of a permanent assistive system. [@FDA-PRECISION-K242618]

The summary describes nonclinical testing addressing the risks of that component, including biocompatibility, electrical/EMC performance, electrode properties, mechanical durability, packaging, sterilisation and shelf life. Examples include the ISO 10993 biological-evaluation framework and ISO 11135 ethylene-oxide sterilisation validation. This evidence demonstrates how an apparently simple array must be translated into a reproducibly manufactured clinical article. The cited standards are those in the historical submission, not a declaration that every current standard or later configuration has been audited. [@FDA-PRECISION-K242618]

Manufacture is unusually visible for an early private company. In October 2023 Precision announced acquisition of a MEMS foundry outside Dallas through Precision BioMEMS. This supports a dated account of bringing fabrication capability under company control. It does not disclose the acquisition cost or establish that every component and final release step is performed there today. [@PRECISION-FACTORY-2023]

For the business, fabrication control could reduce dependence on external capacity and help iteration, but it also adds fixed costs, process-control obligations and yield risk. Those consequences are analysis of the operating model, not measured results of the acquisition. Market entry still depends on reproducibility and quality alongside recording performance.

Historical FDA letters refer to the former Quality System regulation. A current US account must recognise the QMSR amendments effective 2 February 2026, incorporating ISO 13485:2016 requirements into 21 CFR Part 820. This regulatory framework does not itself verify Precision's current compliance. UK/EU authorisation, current factory arrangements and complete quality documentation were not established in this review. [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

The temporary component's buyer and financial value proposition need to be established before considering payment for future assistive BCI use. The immediate analytical model is a hospital acquiring an electrode for a clinical procedure. The clinician values reliable information; procurement evaluates compatibility, price and supply; the hospital must decide whether better care or operational value justifies its incremental expenditure. These interests need not align with an eventual home-use BCI market.

CMS explains that some integral outpatient items are packaged within payment for the main hospital service. That is a route to investigate, not evidence that Layer 7-T has a specific packaged payment or coverage determination. Setting matters: an inpatient procedure, an outpatient service and a research use can have different financing arrangements. No product-specific fee, policy, price or procurement contract was verified. [@CMS-PAYMENT-SYSTEMS]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Patient] -->|clinical need| C[Neurosurgical team]
  C -->|recording information and care| P
  M[Precision] -->|electrode and support| H[Hospital]
  H -->|purchase decision| M
  C -->|technical and clinical requirements| H
  Y[Payer or commissioner] -.->|payment depends on service and eligibility| H
  R[Regulator] -->|market conditions| M
```

*Figure 1. Analytical stakeholder map for temporary clinical use. Dashed payment is conditional; this figure does not document a Layer 7-T payer contract. The lecture-specific map format has not been supplied.*

A procurement case would compare incremental acquisition and implementation costs against measured clinical benefit and any usable resource savings. It should include compatibility with existing recording systems and the cost of interpretation, rather than treating the electrode as the whole service. A research collaboration may provide early experience, but research expenditure is not evidence of routine clinical reimbursement.

No London product user was verified. A remote discussion with an inventor or company clinical lead could clarify the original design and intended purchasing pathway, but willingness to talk and access to confidential budgets remain unknown. No interview has occurred. The absence of verified local use in this search should not be presented as evidence that no UK activity exists.

## Conclusion

Precision provides a strong example of the difficulty of defining the commercial unit in a platform company. A cleared temporary electrode, candidate array/insertion IP, disclosed early capital and a manufacturing acquisition form a coherent development story. The main unresolved step is showing how a particular clinical service pays for, uses and benefits from the component. A persuasive final case study should retain that boundary throughout; using future BCI benefits to justify current electrode economics would weaken every section. The report is useful for examining staged translation, but its eligible population, complete original IP/employment chain and actual procurement economics require further evidence.

reports.title: Building a closed-loop therapy for focal epilepsy
reports.scope: Original US RNS focal-epilepsy pathway; later model/UK questions kept separate
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

NeuroPace's RNS System is a relatively complete public case of translating responsive brain stimulation into a clinical product. It records intracranial electrical activity, detects configured patterns and delivers stimulation for selected adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. The business depends on more than the implant: patient localisation, surgery, programming and follow-up are integral to treatment. Original FDA evidence, long-term outcomes, a pre-approval financing filing, manufacturing disclosure, an economic model and a payer policy allow those elements to be connected. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

The evidence is strongest for the original US focal-epilepsy case. It is less complete for the earliest financing, employment and ownership at invention, and routine UK access. The report therefore uses the US pathway as its main commercial setting and treats London first-hand access as an unresolved practical limitation. It does not combine investigational indications with the original market.

## Device and case boundaries

RNS combines intracranial electrodes with a cranially implanted neurostimulator and external programming/data equipment. Clinicians configure detection and stimulation around the patient's seizure patterns. Sensing and intervention form a feedback loop; the clinician still selects patients, interprets recordings and adjusts therapy. This makes the product a continuing treatment service rather than a single surgical transaction. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

The original indication concerns adults aged at least 18 with partial/focal-onset seizures localised to no more than two foci and refractory to at least two antiseizure medicines. The original evidence covers frequent disabling seizures, averaging at least three monthly over the preceding three months, with no month below two. This report follows that scope, distinguishes the randomised evidence from later open-label follow-up, and separates historic implant models where labeling differs. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

## 1. Unmet medical need

The relevant problem is persistent disabling seizures despite treatment, particularly where seizure localisation and the suitability of other surgery constrain options. Counting everyone with epilepsy would substantially overstate the RNS market. In the 2021 US National Health Interview Survey, Kobau and colleagues estimated 2,865,000 adults, or 1.1%, with active epilepsy. The reported definition combines a doctor diagnosis with treatment and/or a seizure during the previous year. This establishes a dated national burden, not the device-eligible subgroup. The repository abstract was reviewed; complete uncertainty and methods require the full paper. [@CDC-EPILEPSY-NHIS2021]

Eligibility then narrows through drug resistance, focal onset, localisation, age and clinical suitability. The original FDA record supplies the treatment boundary. It cannot, by itself, identify how many survey respondents meet every criterion. A defensible unmet-need section should show this narrowing explicitly rather than multiply the broad prevalence by an unsupported adoption percentage. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

The pivotal randomised study involved 191 implanted participants. During the blinded evaluation, seizure frequency decreased by 37.9% in the active group versus 17.3% in the sham group. This supports a treatment effect beyond implantation and expectation during that period. Nine-year prospective follow-up reports a 75% median reduction, but it is an open-label result with a different design and time frame. The two percentages should not be presented as successive randomised comparisons. [@RNS-TRIAL] [@RNS-LONG]

The clinical proposition is meaningful seizure reduction rather than a guaranteed cure. Benefits must be weighed against implantation and continuing management. A payer or patient also needs to know which outcomes matter beyond frequency: adverse events, functional consequences, quality of life and the burden of repeated care. The original review and long-term evidence support that discussion; they do not eliminate individual variation or establish superiority over every other intervention.

The cost comparison is likewise a pathway comparison. Continued medicines, epilepsy-related care, implantation, programming and replacement all belong in an economic assessment. A published model considers these components, but no observed UK before/after expenditure study was verified here. Clinical improvement, health-economic value and cash savings should remain separate conclusions.

## 2. Intellectual property

US6016449A provides a foundational invention trail. Published in January 2000 from a 1997 filing, it names Robert Fischell, David Fischell and Adrian Upton. A Johns Hopkins historical account identifies Robert Fischell as NeuroPace's founder and describes his earlier Applied Physics Laboratory career. This biographical evidence does not establish his employer when the patent was filed or demonstrate a Johns Hopkins licence. [@RNS-PATENT] [@RNS-JHU-FOUNDER]

The granted publication contains two independent claims, both read for this draft.

| Claim | Main content and connection |
|---|---|
| 1 | Intracranial electrodes connected to a module implanted beneath the scalp; brain-derived inputs govern stimulation outputs, and external equipment communicates in both directions to retrieve data and define outputs intended to terminate a neurological event. This explains the basic responsive-stimulation architecture. |
| 46 | A similar electrode/module/external-communication architecture, with an additional remotely implanted sensor/actuator and its circuitry. That additional requirement should not be assumed present in the commercial RNS configuration. |

*Table 1. Independent claims in the selected foundational patent. The claim elements are summarised; this is not an infringement or freedom-to-operate opinion.* [@RNS-PATENT]

The first claim is useful because it connects the product's sensing, processing, stimulation and external programming functions. The second shows why an IP report must read every independent claim rather than describe the entire patent as one broad idea. Different independent claims protect different combinations, and a commercial product may relate more closely to some than others.

The Google record indicates lifetime expiry, so this historical patent should not be presented as an enduring present-day barrier. The 2021 prospectus also describes trade secrets, confidentiality and invention-assignment agreements. Those disclosures support a broader protection strategy, while leaving the technical contents of undisclosed know-how unknown. Later patents and exact current-product coverage require separate analysis. [@RNS-PATENT] [@RNS-S1]

The public material therefore supports a credible invention narrative and explanation of the selected independent claims. It does not complete the original employer/assignment chain or a current portfolio map. A founder's earlier university association is insufficient to fill those gaps.

## 3. Fundraising

NeuroPace's pre-approval funding is partly recoverable from securities records. A Form D signed on 30 August 2011 reports a first sale on 16 August, $49,126,004 sold and a total offering of $61,914,481. The security categories include equity and options/related securities. The amount sold and the total offered must be separated; neither can automatically be described as a completed all-cash round. [@RNS-FORMD-2011]

The timing is commercially informative. The patent trail reaches back to the late 1990s, the company reports incorporation in November 1997, and original FDA approval arrived in November 2013. The 2011 filing captures a development-period financing event within a much longer translation effort. It is not the first-ever funding record and does not establish what each investor paid or how capital was allocated. [@RNS-PATENT] [@RNS-S1] [@RNS-FORMD-2011] [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

The extended route helps explain why financing and clinical/regulatory milestones must be analysed together. An implanted feedback system needs engineering verification, manufacturing controls, surgery and sustained clinical evaluation. Capital may have to support several of these activities before product sales can repay them. This is an interpretation of the documented development demands, not an assertion that the 2011 proceeds financed a particular trial invoice.

The 2021 IPO prospectus is a later disclosure route into company operations and financial history. Its existence makes detailed investigation easier, but later public-market finance should not replace the missing earliest-round story. The prospectus's revenues, operating expenses and financing entries also concern the company and relevant periods, rather than a retrospective price tag for inventing RNS. [@RNS-S1]

No defensible pre-/post-money valuation or complete first-stage capital requirement was established. A bottom-up estimate would need staff-years, prototype iterations, implant verification, trial-site and follow-up costs, regulatory expenditure and manufacturing setup through an agreed endpoint. A top-down comparison should use another implantable closed-loop therapy at a comparable stage, rather than a noninvasive EEG device. Without verified unit costs or matched comparables, a numerical estimate would add apparent precision rather than evidence. The financing section is informative but not a complete funding reconstruction.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

RNS obtained original US PMA approval on 14 November 2013 under P100026. The implanted system followed the Class III/PMA route, supported by device testing and clinical evidence. Its original focal-epilepsy indication and eligibility restrictions are central to the business: market size and payer eligibility depend on them. The randomised pivotal evidence supplies more than a company assertion of benefit. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

The original FDA review covers biological evaluation, implanted-system and external-equipment testing, sterilisation and clinical safety/effectiveness. Examples include ISO 10993 biological testing and ethylene-oxide validation under the then-cited ISO 11135-1 framework. The relevant engineering problem is sustained safe operation in a patient, including materials, hermeticity, electrical function and reliable communication. These historical test records do not establish that every later model or indication has identical evidence. [@FDA-RNS-P100026]

Model-specific changes matter. The February 2020 Rev 6 MRI manual distinguishes MR Conditional RNS-320 from MR Unsafe RNS-300M, with the former subject to specified conditions. A blanket statement that “RNS cannot undergo MRI” would therefore misrepresent the later model. Conversely, “MR Conditional” is not permission for any scan in any circumstances. This report uses the distinction to illustrate label evolution, not to give scanning instructions. [@RNS-MRI-2020]

Manufacturing is described in the April 2021 prospectus: assembly, testing, inspection and final release took place at Mountain View, California, with materials, subassemblies and services supplied externally, often from single sources. That account supports a mixed in-house/supplier operating model. It also exposes a commercial risk: qualifying a replacement supplier may take time, so component availability can constrain delivery even where final assembly is internal. It is a dated disclosure, not a current factory audit. [@RNS-S1]

For present US context, the QMSR amendments became effective on 2 February 2026 and incorporate ISO 13485:2016 requirements into Part 820. This should be distinguished from the former QS terminology in older records. A complete current UK/EU authorisation and manufacturing assessment was not undertaken. No London RNS user or routine NHS payment route was verified. [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

RNS has both a public economic argument and an identifiable payer policy, which answer different questions. Youngerman and colleagues modelled RNS plus continued medicines versus medicines alone over nine years from a public-payer perspective. Across three utility estimates, the reported incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was $28,825–$46,596 per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY). The model includes implantation, programming, replacement, adverse events and care costs. The publisher abstract was reviewed; this is a model result, not a hospital purchase price or observed budget saving. [@RNS-ECON-PUBLISHER]

Aetna CPB 0394, reviewed in June 2026, identifies responsive cortical stimulation as medically necessary for selected adults under specified criteria. These include localising no more than two epileptogenic regions, adequate trials of at least two antiseizure medicines and further clinical/surgical requirements. The entire policy and individual plan terms matter. This establishes one US payer's position rather than universal insurer or NHS coverage. [@AETNA-RNS-0394]

The model helps explain value over time, while the policy shows how a payer translates evidence into eligibility. A successful implant is still followed by programming and long-term management. The provider must organise those services, and the payer must decide how the episode and continuing care are funded. A favourable ICER cannot establish the actual payment amount or the provider's margin.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Eligible patient] -->|assessment and follow-up| E[Epilepsy centre]
  E -->|localisation, implantation and programming| P
  N[NeuroPace] -->|implant and technical support| E
  E -->|purchasing relationship| N
  I[Insurer] -.->|covered services subject to criteria| E
  F[FDA] -->|authorised indication and conditions| N
```

*Figure 1. Analytical stakeholder map for the US focal-epilepsy pathway. The payer arrow is conditional; the Aetna policy establishes selected coverage criteria, not every contract or fee. The lecture-specific map format remains unavailable.*

The central adoption issue is the alignment of a substantial intervention now with benefits accumulated over years. The economic result depends on durable seizure improvement, utility mapping and the costs of continuing treatment. It is therefore important to examine sensitivity rather than repeat a single ICER as a universal conclusion. A UK adaptation would need NHS costs, relevant commissioning and local eligible patients; a currency conversion of the US model would be inadequate.

For first-hand investigation, a product-specific US clinical or development lead can address actual selection and follow-up. A London epilepsy expert could be useful only through a specific relevant clinical/purchasing question; general expertise does not establish RNS experience. No conversation or visit has occurred.

## Conclusion

RNS offers the most connected public development-to-treatment account in this set: a defined clinical group, original randomised evidence, longer follow-up, a foundational claim set, pre-approval financing, manufacturing disclosure, a value model and payer criteria. Its entrepreneurial lesson is that a closed-loop implant reaches patients through an equally important clinical and financial service loop. The remaining weaknesses concern the very earliest finance and invention arrangements, current full portfolio/label coverage and UK access. These limits reduce completeness, but do not prevent a substantive case study grounded in a coherent original US market.

reports.title: Turning EEG access into an acute-care product
reports.scope: Original rapid-EEG hardware/sonification and its evolution; later software and payment distinguished
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

Ceribell's early commercial proposition was rapid access to interpretable brain activity in acute care. The original product combined a quickly applied EEG headband, a portable recorder and a sound-based representation of brain signals. Later software added automated analysis. The case is strongest when those generations are traced separately: clinical workflow, university-origin sonification, early finance, hardware clearance and later software/payment developments form related but distinct events. [@CERIBELL-RECORDER-K170363] [@CERIBELL-HEADBAND-K171459] [@FDA-CERIBELL-K223504]

Public records support an unusually detailed academic-to-company narrative, including Stanford seed support and licence terms. Evidence that rapid EEG changes access and clinical decisions is stronger than evidence of realised cash savings. A further complication is time: the US inpatient new-technology add-on for the seizure monitor ends in FY2027. Sustainable adoption therefore needs an economic case beyond a temporary supplement. [@CMS-IPPS-FY2027]

## Device and case boundaries

The headband places electrodes on the scalp without an invasive procedure. The recorder displays signals and supplies an audio representation that trained clinicians can interpret. It is designed to make EEG information available during an acute decision, while conventional EEG may require a technologist and specialist interpretation. The original recorder's label did not provide an automatic diagnostic conclusion or adverse-event alert. [@CERIBELL-RECORDER-K170363]

The later Status Epilepticus Monitor belongs to a software development pathway. Evidence or authorisation for that version should not be read backwards as proof of the original system's AI performance. This report centres on the original rapid-EEG business and follows later software only where it explains commercial evolution and payment. It also keeps the separate delirium-monitor decision outside the seizure-monitor indication.

## 1. Unmet medical need

Some critically ill patients have seizure activity without obvious convulsions. Decisions made before EEG can involve the competing risks of missing ongoing activity or treating a presumed seizure unnecessarily. The 2015 ACNS consensus describes selected critical-care indications for continuous EEG and the staffing/resource constraints on its delivery. It supplies clinical-pathway context, not Ceribell-specific effectiveness or a universal seizure prevalence for all ICU patients. [@ACNS-CCEEG-2015]

The unmet need is consequently an information-and-access problem within a defined care pathway. A patient can need a timely EEG decision even if no seizure is ultimately found. Estimating the addressable population from all epilepsy diagnoses would miss that feature and include many people outside the intended acute-care use. No reliable UK count of the relevant suspected-seizure episodes was established here; this remains a quantitative population gap.

DECIDE provides direct workflow evidence. It was a prospective observational study involving 181 ICU patient encounters, with complete clinical/EEG information available for 164. It reported median rapid-EEG acquisition of five minutes and conventional-EEG delay of 239 minutes, with available numbers varying by measure. The assessment concerned physician decisions and interpretations, not an autonomous AI diagnosis. It was funded by Ceribell and disclosed relevant company relationships. [@CERIBELL-DECIDE]

The study makes a plausible commercial mechanism concrete: information becomes available during a period when clinicians otherwise face uncertainty. However, it does not randomise hospitals to different care systems or demonstrate a causal reduction in mortality or length of stay. A separate 38-patient emergency-care pilot contained only one nonconvulsive status epilepticus case. Its nominal 100% sensitivity therefore had a very wide confidence interval, reported as 5%–100%, and cannot justify a broad perfect-detection claim. [@CERIBELL-ED]

For a hospital, the relevant comparison is a pathway: rapid access plus appropriate escalation to further monitoring versus the existing diagnostic process. A reduced-montage early assessment and longer conventional monitoring can serve different functions. The economic value depends on whether earlier information changes treatment correctly, not simply whether more recordings are made.

No prospective before/after cost study was verified in this research. A Ceribell-specific model supplies useful economic reasoning, discussed below, but its predicted expenditure changes should not be presented as measured savings. The clinical evidence supports an access and decision-making case more firmly than a completed outcomes-and-cost case.

## 2. Intellectual property

The original sonification feature has a clear Stanford connection. US10136862B2, *Method of sonifying brain electrical activity*, names Christopher Chafe and Josef Parvizi, with priority from May 2012 and grant publication in November 2018. The university's origin account connects their work to Ceribell. This is more specific than a general claim that the company owns “EEG AI.” [@CERIBELL-PATENT] [@CERIBELL-ORIGIN]

All four independent claims in the selected granted publication were read.

| Claim | Main content |
|---|---|
| 1 | A method that filters a brain signal and continuously controls several sound parameters, including vowel, intensity and pitch, driving audible synthesis for diagnosis/treatment. |
| 18 | A processor system with signal acquisition, conversion/filtering, modulators, synthesis and a speaker implementing the sonification arrangement. |
| 20 | A system expressed through processor, memory and program instructions performing the signal-to-sound operations and playback. |
| 26 | A method using vocal synthesis in which the audible representation varies across stages of a brain-activity event. |

*Table 1. Independent claims in US10136862B2. These protect specified sonification arrangements, not every headband design or later seizure-classification algorithm.* [@CERIBELL-PATENT]

The related licence record is unusually informative. An amendment effective April 2017 identifies the June 2015 Stanford agreement and technology dockets S11-220, S13-470 and 14-459 from the Parvizi/Chafe labs. It discloses a $36,000 first-commercial-sale milestone, while royalty percentages are redacted. A June 2025 filing reports a $250,000 payment to extend exclusivity through expiry of the last licensed patent. [@CERIBELL-STANFORD-LICENCE-2017] [@CERIBELL-STANFORD-LICENCE-2025]

Those records establish a contractual technology-transfer relationship and a dated commercial obligation. They do not prove that the selected patent covers every marketed feature, nor disclose the complete economics of the licence. The docket-to-family and product-to-claim map still needs completion, particularly for later Clarity software. Likewise, academic laboratory affiliation supports origin but is not a complete employment-record audit.

The entrepreneurial lesson is that usable IP can reach a company through a licence rather than a simple claim of outright ownership. Commercialisation must support both development expenditure and contractual obligations. The stated milestone and exclusivity payment belong in that analysis; they are payments associated with rights, not investment capital raised by Ceribell.

## 3. Fundraising

Stanford Bio-X attributes Ceribell's creation to a Round 6, 2012 interdisciplinary seed grant for the Parvizi/Chafe project converting brain waves to sound and image. The university account identifies support for the research stage but gives no amount. The research grant should therefore appear before corporate finance without being invented as a company seed-equity valuation. [@CERIBELL-BIOX-SEED]

The August 2024 S-1 offers a more detailed early company history. Note 10 reports $1.0 million net Series Seed proceeds across August 2015 and April 2016, $2.0 million of convertible-note cash in 2016, and $7.0 million net Series A proceeds in the second quarter of 2017. The notes converted in May 2017. Conversion does not create the same cash a second time. [@CERIBELL-S1-AUG2024]

| Stage | Publicly supported financing | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Academic origin, 2012 | Bio-X seed grant; amount not disclosed | Academic project support. |
| 2015–2016 | $1.0m net Series Seed | Company proceeds, not total invention cost. |
| 2016 | $2.0m convertible-note cash | Later conversion must not be double-counted. |
| Q2 2017 | $7.0m net Series A | Net proceeds differ from gross round announcements. |
| 2018 | $35m Series B announced | Later commercial development finance. |

*Table 2. Academic support and corporate financing stages. Original US-dollar amounts are retained. The stages should not be summed into a verified device-development budget.* [@CERIBELL-BIOX-SEED] [@CERIBELL-S1-AUG2024] [@CERIBELL-FIN]

The 2018 Series B announcement names Optimas Capital Partners Fund and The Rise Fund as leads. It helps explain later scale-up, but the earlier filing entries are more useful for the first commercial product. Together with the hardware clearances, the record supports a staged academic-research, prototype, commercial-entry and expansion narrative. It does not establish how much each activity cost. [@CERIBELL-FIN]

Important financing details remain private or unverified: the academic grant value, early pre-/post-money valuations, founders' non-cash contributions and expenditure attributable to particular hardware/software generations. A bottom-up reconstruction would allocate development staff, headband/recorder prototypes, software, clinical validation, regulatory work and manufacturing setup to a defined first-version endpoint. A top-down comparison would require another acute-care EEG business with comparable hardware, software and trial demands. No attributable cost inputs were verified, so the report supplies a documented financing timeline rather than a fabricated original R&D total.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

The original US hardware records give a more accurate starting point than a later AI clearance alone. K170363 describes the pocket EEG recorder; K171459 covers the Class II cutaneous EEG headband, cleared in August 2017, with an age-six-and-above indication in that historical label. The recorder's eight-channel visual/audio function and lack of automatic diagnostic conclusions distinguish that generation from later event-detection software. [@CERIBELL-RECORDER-K170363] [@CERIBELL-HEADBAND-K171459]

K223504 concerns the later Ceribell Status Epilepticus Monitor under the Class II EEG software pathway. The classification, intended use and validation evidence belong to that configuration. A later software record cannot establish a universal claim about every earlier headband or all current products. A strong regulatory narrative is therefore a sequence of components and intended uses, rather than a single statement that “Ceribell is FDA approved.” [@FDA-CERIBELL-K223504]

The validation questions follow the component risks. The original recorder summary cites EEG safety/performance under IEC 60601-2-26, electrical/EMC work under IEC 60601-1 and IEC 60601-1-2, and battery testing under IEC 62133. The headband record describes patient-contact cytotoxicity, sensitisation and irritation evaluation under the then-cited ISO 10993-5/10993-10 editions. These are actual component records, not a generic standards list. They remain historical evidence rather than a complete current conformity assessment of every later software configuration. [@CERIBELL-RECORDER-K170363] [@CERIBELL-HEADBAND-K171459]

Manufacturing disclosure improves the account. The 2024 filing describes third-party headband manufacture in China and recorder final assembly in Sunnyvale, California, alongside reliance on contract manufacturers. This supports a concrete outsourced/in-house split at that date. It also identifies a business dependency: a recurring consumable and a capital recorder have different supply and scale-up requirements. Current factories, supplier contracts and the complete quality system were not audited. [@CERIBELL-S1-AUG2024]

The US QMSR amendments effective February 2026 provide the current Part 820 quality framework, incorporating ISO 13485:2016 requirements. This context should not be confused with a certificate or proof of Ceribell's compliance. UK/EU market entry, exact current software indications and a licensed London user were not verified in this review. [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

The economic argument is that faster correct information can avoid unnecessary treatment or prolonged care. Ney, Gururangan and Parvizi modelled rapid EEG versus clinical suspicion using diagnostic information, literature and US inpatient cost inputs indexed to 2019 dollars. Their probabilistic analysis reported approximately $5,633 savings per use case and cost savings in 75% of replications. These are modeled findings, not money observed in hospital accounts. Ceribell funded the work, and the authors disclosed founder/advisory relationships. [@CERIBELL-ECON]

The model is useful because it exposes the causal chain that purchasing depends on: information changes decisions, decisions change resource use, and resource changes have economic consequences. Its weakest step for a local hospital is transferability. Different staffing, availability of conventional EEG, admission patterns and bed constraints can change the result. Bed capacity released is also not equivalent to an immediate cash reduction. A hospital would need its own volumes, variable costs and actual product terms.

Payment evidence introduces an additional timing issue. The FY2027 IPPS final rule discontinues the NTAP for the Ceribell Status Epilepticus Monitor. It separately approves a Ceribell Delirium Monitor System for FY2027. The latter is not a renewal of the seizure-monitor award. NTAP expiry does not mean that every underlying hospital service ceases to be paid. [@CMS-IPPS-FY2027]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Patient with suspected seizure] -->|urgent assessment| H[Acute-care hospital]
  H -->|EEG-informed care| P
  C[Ceribell] -->|recorder, headbands and software| H
  H -->|purchase or commercial terms| C
  N[Neurology and critical-care teams] -->|interpretation and escalation| H
  Y[Payer] -.->|eligible hospital-service payment| H
  U[Stanford] -->|licensed technology| C
```

*Figure 1. Analytical stakeholder map for acute-care rapid EEG. The licence relationship is documented; the purchasing/payment arrows do not assert a particular current contract. Lecture-specific map formatting remains to be confirmed.*

This leaves a substantive commercial question after temporary support ends: does the hospital's own clinical and operational value justify the recorder, consumables, software and training? No verified current price, subscription agreement, hospital contract or routine NHS coverage was identified. A favourable economic model cannot answer those transaction questions by itself.

No London Ceribell user was verified. Josef Parvizi is relevant as a product inventor and economic-paper author, with a specific connection to origin and model assumptions. General EEG expertise alone would not justify naming another local academic as a substitute for device experience. No interview was conducted, so the report contains no personal-communication evidence.

## Conclusion

Ceribell supports a persuasive case about making a specialist diagnostic resource available during an urgent clinical decision. Academic seed support, sonification claims, licence terms, early company proceeds, component clearances and supply-chain disclosure create a substantial original-development account. The main uncertainty is how strongly better access translates into patient outcomes and sustainable local economics. The public evidence supports workflow improvement and a testable value proposition; realised savings, exact current purchasing terms and the post-NTAP payment model remain less complete. Maintaining the original-hardware/later-software boundary is essential to keeping the story accurate.

reports.title: Commercialising a personalised five-day TMS pathway
reports.scope: Academic-to-commercial SAINT and original US clearance; UK comparator context kept separate
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

Magnus Medical's SAINT case concerns commercialising an integrated treatment pathway: personalised MRI-based targeting, navigated magnetic stimulation and a compressed five-day schedule. Its proposition is faster delivery of a potentially effective intervention for adults whose depression has not improved satisfactorily with medication. The entrepreneurial challenge is to turn a small, promising academic evidence base into a reproducible, staffed and sustainably funded service. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The public record connects Stanford-origin IP and research support to a $25 million company launch round, FDA clearance and a named hardware supplier. It is less complete for long-term service economics and current payer arrangements. The expiry of the temporary US inpatient NTAP for FY2027 makes those economics especially relevant. A short treatment calendar should not be mistaken for a low-resource treatment, nor should UK evidence for another TMS protocol be described as SAINT evidence. [@CMS-IPPS-FY2027]

## Device and case boundaries

The Magnus Neuromodulation System with SAINT technology combines stimulation hardware, neuronavigation and software informed by structural and functional MRI. It identifies a personalised target in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and delivers intermittent theta-burst stimulation. The cleared protocol compresses a course into five days, using multiple sessions per day. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The original US clearance concerns adult major depressive disorder with inadequate improvement from antidepressant medication in the current episode. This report studies the academic-to-commercial transition through that 2022 clearance and subsequent service development. It does not equate every accelerated TMS protocol, MRI-guided TMS clinic or MagVenture installation with the licensed SAINT configuration.

## 1. Unmet medical need

Depression creates substantial global burden, but the relevant unmet need is narrower than the total disease population. WHO's September 2026 fact sheet reports approximately 322 million people with depression in 2023 and an adult prevalence of 5.2%. These figures are global context. They do not count people eligible for SAINT, quantify treatment resistance in London or establish capacity to receive an MRI-plus-stimulation pathway. [@WHO-DEPRESSION-2026]

The clinical development addresses people with persistent symptoms despite previous care. A commercially useful need statement must connect inadequate treatment response with the time, access and tolerability demands of available alternatives. The specific attraction of acceleration is that repeated treatment visits are concentrated into a shorter calendar period. Whether that improves access depends on the patient and service: fewer weeks of travel can coexist with long daily attendance and demanding staff schedules.

The original FDA summary includes a double-blind sham-controlled study of 29 participants, 14 active and 15 sham. It reports remission in 11/14 active participants versus 2/15 sham participants during the month after treatment and notes early termination at the planned interim analysis. The small sample and short observation period limit generalisation. The summary's study tables also contain an inconsistent active/sham header in one place, so this draft uses the consistent 14-active/15-sham description in the study narrative and table rows. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

These findings support a serious clinical-development argument, but they do not establish durable remission for all treated patients or superiority over unrelated interventions through cross-trial percentages. Larger implementation populations, follow-up, retreatment and patient selection affect both clinical and commercial conclusions. The early trial's apparent effect should therefore remain attached to its actual design and denominator.

A UK comparison helps make the care-pathway problem concrete. The NIHR BRIGhTMIND trial randomised 255 people with treatment-resistant depression between connectivity-guided iTBS and rTMS, delivered over 20 sessions in four to six weeks. It found no superiority of its connectivity-guided intervention and had no sham group. That protocol is different from SAINT. Its relevance is the organisation of an existing UK TMS pathway, not evidence that SAINT has the same efficacy, costs or availability. The report abstract was checked; the full appendices were not audited. [@SAINT-NIHR-COMPARATOR]

A UK eligible-patient count and observed before/after cost comparison for SAINT were not verified. The unmet-need case is clinically plausible and supported by early direct evidence, while population sizing and local service impact remain incomplete.

## 2. Intellectual property

The academic origin is supported by both the company and the university. Stanford's technology-transfer report describes the Williams laboratory invention, Magnus commercialisation and assistance with the patent strategy. US10595735B2 names Nolan Williams and Keith Sudheimer, with Stanford as assignee and priority from January 2018. Magnus identifies that publication among its licensed patents. This supports a specific institutional transfer narrative, while leaving the full licence terms and contemporaneous employment records unverified. [@SAINT-STANFORD-OTL2022] [@SAINT-PATENT] [@SAINT-IP]

All four independent claims in the selected granted patent were read.

| Claim | Main content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Personalised accelerated intermittent TBS targeting, stimulation over consecutive days and multiple daily sessions, with unstimulated intervals of 25–120 minutes and defined pulse-train structure. |
| 10 | A corresponding accelerated continuous-TBS treatment method with daily sessions separated by unstimulated intervals of 10–50 minutes. |
| 19 | An intermittent-TBS system configured for consecutive days and multiple daily sessions separated by 10–50-minute unstimulated intervals, with the specified train structure. |
| 24 | A continuous-TBS system configured for the corresponding multi-day/session arrangement and 10–50-minute intervals. |

*Table 1. Independent claims in US10595735B2. Intermittent and continuous variants must be distinguished; the commercial cleared protocol uses iTBS. Short descriptions do not replace each complete claim.* [@SAINT-PATENT]

The claims show why the IP story is more specific than ownership of “TMS for depression.” They concern combinations of targeting, schedule and stimulation structure. They also extend beyond the particular commercial intermittent protocol to continuous variants. Patent scope and authorised clinical use are separate boundaries.

Commercial value can arise from integrating the protected method with software, navigation and delivery support. However, no complete mapping of each commercial feature to the patent family, later improvements or supplier rights was completed. The university account confirms involvement, not an independently verified royalty schedule or freedom-to-operate position. Reported IP enforcement provides a further company-history lead, but this draft does not assert a court outcome from a manufacturer's account. [@SAINT-IP]

## 3. Fundraising

SAINT has two funding histories that should not be collapsed: academic research support and company equity. Stanford's October 2021 account identifies a Brain & Behavior Research Foundation Young Investigator Award and philanthropic support, including named Schwab and Chao funds. The account supplies funder identities but not attributable award amounts. It supports the research stage without establishing Magnus's capitalisation. [@SAINT-ACADEMIC-FUNDERS]

In October 2021 Magnus announced a $25 million Series A, co-led by JAZZ Venture Partners and Red Tree Venture Capital, alongside its Stanford licence and development plans. The release's header and body differ by one day, so this report uses month/year rather than selecting an unsupported precise event date. No pre-/post-money valuation or complete earlier financing history was disclosed in the reviewed record. [@SAINT-SERIESA-2021]

| Stage | Evidence | What can be concluded |
|---|---|---|
| Academic development | Named research award and philanthropic support | The study had identifiable external support; attributable amounts remain unknown. |
| Company launch, October 2021 | $25m Series A; named co-leads | Capital was announced for commercial development, not a measured total cost of inventing SAINT. |
| Clearance, September 2022 | K220177 | A later regulatory milestone; no source allocates a specific amount of the round to it. |

*Table 2. Research support, corporate capital and a later milestone. The rows are related chronologically, but do not prove how the money was spent.* [@SAINT-ACADEMIC-FUNDERS] [@SAINT-SERIESA-2021] [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The financing story is a translation from an academic method to a supported system and delivery business. That requires more than repeating a laboratory result: software development, reproducible target identification, integration with hardware, validation, training and service support create additional needs. The $25 million announcement is evidence of capital raised, while those activities explain possible capital requirements. Their actual expenditure is not publicly reconstructed here.

A bottom-up estimate should separate precommercial academic work from company integration and market-entry costs, using staff-years, software verification, trial costs and supplier/integration expenditure. A top-down comparator should resemble an MRI-informed TMS service, not an implanted BCI. Without verified effort, award amounts or comparable attributable budgets, this draft does not put a speculative dollar total on the missing early work. The named funders and round provide a useful account, but not complete original financing or valuation.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

FDA cleared the Magnus system under K220177 on 1 September 2022 as a Class II repetitive TMS system under 21 CFR 882.5805. The record names a predicate system and includes the commercial hardware/software configuration, intended users and supporting studies. Clearance concerns that defined system and indication, not an interchangeable collection of TMS equipment and targeting software. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The submission describes biological evaluation under ISO 10993-1, software lifecycle work including IEC 62304, risk management under ISO 14971, and electrical/EMC, performance and usability evaluation. The engineering burden follows from integration: a target calculated from MRI must translate into reproducible coil placement and correctly delivered stimulation. The safety case therefore includes software and workflow as well as the coil itself. These are historical submission records, not a complete present-day conformity assessment. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The clearance summary also describes a course of 50 ten-minute sessions, totalling 500 minutes of active stimulation over five days. Calendar compression therefore does not mean a few brief staff contacts: intersession gaps, navigation, assessment and patient attendance sit around the stimulation time. This resource implication is important to the reimbursement case. It is calculated from the documented schedule, not a measured staffing study. [@FDA-SAINT-K220177]

The supply chain is partly identifiable. MagVenture confirms supplying the MagPro magnetic-stimulation system and supporting installation/service for SAINT. Its page header and body have different dates, retained in the source notes. The named relationship is stronger evidence than a generic supplier capability page, but does not identify every manufacturing responsibility or prove that all MagVenture-equipped clinics deliver SAINT. [@SAINT-MAGVENTURE]

Current US quality context includes the QMSR amendments effective February 2026, incorporating ISO 13485:2016 requirements into Part 820. The reviewed material does not establish a complete current UK/EU authorisation, quality audit or licensed London SAINT site. General local TMS experience can inform service questions, but cannot stand in for exact-product delivery experience. [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

SAINT's economic unit is a pathway containing MRI, target analysis, navigation, repeated stimulation, professional supervision and follow-up. Payment for one element does not establish funding for the complete package. A hospital or clinic must compare the cost and capacity requirements with the clinical benefits and the applicable payer arrangement in its actual setting.

The FY2027 US IPPS final rule discontinues SAINT's temporary inpatient NTAP after the relevant new-technology window. This is a material update to older manufacturer descriptions of support. It does not demonstrate that all base inpatient payment ends or settle outpatient/private coverage. A report should identify the payment mechanism and year, rather than describe NTAP as a permanent product-wide reimbursement entitlement. [@CMS-IPPS-FY2027]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Eligible patient] -->|assessment and attendance| C[Treatment service]
  C -->|targeted TMS and follow-up| P
  I[MRI and targeting workflow] -->|patient-specific target| C
  M[Magnus] -->|system, software and support| C
  V[MagVenture] -->|stimulation hardware and service| M
  U[Stanford] -->|licensed technology| M
  Y[Payer or patient] -.->|setting-specific payment| C
```

*Figure 1. Analytical stakeholder map for SAINT delivery. Named licence and supplier relationships are supported by their records; the conditional payment arrow does not establish a verified package tariff. The lecture's required map format remains unavailable.*

The key economic trade-off is between faster calendar delivery and concentrated resources. Acceleration may reduce weeks of travel and waiting for completion, while personalisation and repeated daily sessions require imaging and operational capacity. Durable benefit, relapse, retreatment and continued care determine whether that up-front resource use represents good value. The small early trial alone cannot supply every long-term parameter.

UK BRIGhTMIND evidence can frame comparator-service questions, but its outcomes and economics should not be imported as SAINT estimates. No verified SAINT-specific UK price, NHS commissioning decision, current package fee or complete cost-effectiveness analysis was established. A local service model would need actual staffing, scanner, software, equipment and follow-up inputs. Merely converting a US price, if one were found, would not answer those questions.

A US co-developer can provide a product-specific route into development and licensing questions. A UK TMS service could discuss relevant capacity and purchasing issues within its own experience. Neither route is an interview until a conversation occurs; no personal communications are claimed here.

## Conclusion

SAINT offers a coherent entrepreneurship case about converting a personalised academic protocol into an integrated clinical system. The source base supports the university-to-company link, selected independent claims, named academic support, a quantified launch round, FDA evidence and a hardware supplier. The most difficult transition in the narrative is from early clinical promise to sustainable service economics. The full treatment resource burden, durability and retreatment, current payer arrangements and UK availability remain less well established. A strong final report should make that transition its central question rather than rely on striking remission percentages or an expired temporary payment route.

reports.title: Making focused-ultrasound thalamotomy a clinical service
reports.scope: Original unilateral essential-tremor market entry, with an England/London service focus
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

Insightec's Exablate Neuro shows how a technically demanding treatment can reach an established specialist service and a defined public commissioning pathway. For medication-refractory essential tremor, MRI-guided focused ultrasound creates a targeted thalamic lesion through the skull. It avoids an implanted stimulator, but requires careful selection, substantial infrastructure and acceptance of a permanent lesion. The original US evidence, an England economic model, an NHS commissioning policy and documented London equipment make the clinical-to-service account unusually tangible. [@FDA-EXABLATE-P150038] [@NHSE-FOCUSED-ULTRASOUND-2020] [@EXABLATE-LONDON]

The harder sections are original brain-device financing and exact first-version IP/manufacturing attribution. A pre-approval company financing event and a relevant aberration-correction patent improve those accounts without completing them. This report centres on unilateral essential-tremor treatment; Parkinsonian tremor has a different evidence and NHS guidance position.

## Device and case boundaries

Exablate Neuro directs energy from an ultrasound array through the skull toward a brain target. MRI supports targeting and temperature monitoring. At a sufficient thermal dose, tissue is ablated, interrupting activity in a selected circuit. Patient feedback and assessment during treatment help the clinical team evaluate effect and adverse symptoms. This is a lesion procedure, not an implanted electrical stimulator or a claim about every experimental form of ultrasound neuromodulation. [@FDA-EXABLATE-P150038]

The system's commercial unit includes the array/control equipment, suitable imaging infrastructure, planning, specialist staff and follow-up. The first US brain indication in 2016 gives a defined market-entry endpoint. Later bilateral and Parkinson's indications require their own decisions and economic evidence, rather than being folded into the original case.

## 1. Unmet medical need

Essential tremor can interfere with activities such as drinking, eating and writing. The relevant unmet group has disabling symptoms despite medication, rather than everyone with visible tremor. The 2022 England model refers to an estimated UK burden of approximately one million people with essential tremor; this is background drawn on by that study, not a newly verified census or a count eligible for Exablate. Clinical severity, medication response, suitability for lesion treatment and infrastructure narrow the population substantially. [@EXABLATE-ENGLAND-MODEL]

The original FDA evidence supplies a more precise treatment population. Its pivotal study included adults aged at least 22 with medication-refractory essential tremor, including inadequate response to appropriate trials of at least two medicines. The primary analysis involved 76 patients, allocated 56 to Exablate and 20 to sham treatment. The review reports mean improvement in its primary composite tremor/motor endpoint at three months of 46.9% with Exablate versus −0.1% with sham. That is a defined trial result, not an outcome prediction for every referred patient. [@FDA-EXABLATE-P150038]

The clinical value is supported by controlled evidence rather than simply the appeal of avoiding an incision. The trade-off remains important: targeted ablation can produce lasting benefit, but a lesion is permanent and neurological adverse effects matter. Suitability also depends on the treatment target, patient characteristics and the feasibility of delivering energy through the skull. These considerations affect both patient access and service throughput.

The relevant alternatives include continued medical care and other specialist procedures. A comparison with deep brain stimulation (DBS) should consider implanted hardware, adjustability, ongoing management, patient suitability and the distinct risks of lesion treatment. Avoiding an implanted generator changes the pathway; it does not eliminate MRI, planning, specialist time or follow-up. The strongest business analysis therefore compares complete pathways rather than device acquisition alone.

Geography materially changes the need. An existing specialist London service makes practical investigation possible, but does not establish that all eligible UK patients can access it promptly. The 2025 London paper explicitly identifies ExAblate equipment, while UCLH describes a relevant service. Waiting lists, referral exclusions, local capacity and current eligible volumes were not verified. These are meaningful remaining questions rather than reasons to invent a national device market from the broad disease estimate. [@EXABLATE-LONDON] [@EXABLATE-UCLH]

## 2. Intellectual property

A candidate enabling invention is US8088067B2, *Tissue aberration corrections in ultrasound therapy*, naming Kobi Vortman and Shuki Vitek, with priority from December 2002 and grant publication in January 2012. The assignment/name history connects it to the Insightec lineage. The technical problem is relevant: intervening tissue can change ultrasound propagation, so accurate focusing requires compensation. Exact commercial implementation, original employment and the defining first brain-device patent family remain unverified. [@EXABLATE-ABERRATION-PATENT]

All four independent claims in the publication were read.

| Claim | Main content |
|---|---|
| 1 | A system combining an array, imaging, tissue-boundary/sound-speed processing and element control to compensate for refraction and propagation differences. |
| 11 | A focusing method that acquires images, identifies tissue boundaries, derives element-specific corrections and delivers acoustic energy accordingly. |
| 21 | A related method that drives the corrected elements long enough to ablate the target. |
| 26 | Computer-readable software instructions performing the image, boundary and correction operations for an ultrasound system. |

*Table 1. Independent claims in the selected aberration-correction patent. System, focusing method, ablation method and software claims express related technical protection; exact Exablate Neuro coverage has not been demonstrated.* [@EXABLATE-ABERRATION-PATENT]

The claim set provides a substantive technical explanation, stronger than simply stating that the company has many patents. It also exposes an attribution problem: a platform invention may support several products and applications. A granted correction method should not automatically be described as the first Exablate Neuro invention or complete protection of the commercial system.

A complete IP account would connect the final system components to each necessary claim element, trace official assignments and investigate earlier/later families covering the array, MR integration and treatment control. The present source base does not establish freedom to operate or current enforceability. Nor does it document the contents of confidential calibration, production or clinical-planning know-how. Those may matter commercially, but should remain hypotheses unless records support them.

## 3. Fundraising

The most useful recovered transaction predates the 2016 US brain approval. An October 2012 investor filing announced a conditional investment agreement of approximately $31.4 million. Its terms distinguish cash from conversion of a GE loan. The December company announcement then reported completion of a $30.9 million Series C, including $27.6 million from GE and $3.3 million from other investors. These records describe agreement and completion stages; adding them would double-count a transaction history. [@EXABLATE-FINANCE-AGREEMENT-2012] [@EXABLATE-FINANCE-CLOSE-2012]

The source quality problem is visible even within a primary record. The October filing's headline gives a $106.4 million post-money valuation, while the body states $104.6 million. This report adopts neither as settled. The discrepancy needs transaction documentation or clarification, rather than an apparently reasonable silent correction. A syndicated copy of the same release would not constitute independent corroboration. [@EXABLATE-FINANCE-AGREEMENT-2012]

The 2012 financing is evidence of company/platform capital during development, not a brain-only budget or the first funding ever received by Insightec. The later $150 million 2024 financing announcement is a growth-stage event well after the original indication. It helps distinguish continued expansion from original development, but cannot fill the missing first-version finance by substitution. [@EXABLATE-FIN]

| Record | What is supported | What remains open |
|---|---|---|
| October 2012 agreement | Conditional terms; mixed cash/conversion | Conflicting valuation; final terms. |
| December 2012 closing | $30.9m completed Series C announced | Brain-specific allocation and actual development spending. |
| 2024 growth round | $150m financing announced | Original early finance, not answered by a later round. |

*Table 2. Selected financing records in original US dollars. The rows are not a cumulative device-development budget.* [@EXABLATE-FINANCE-AGREEMENT-2012] [@EXABLATE-FINANCE-CLOSE-2012] [@EXABLATE-FIN]

The system requires investment in acoustic control, imaging integration, treatment verification, clinical work and a service ecosystem. A useful bottom-up reconstruction would allocate those activities to the first brain indication, separating shared platform investment from indication-specific work. A top-down check would use a similarly infrastructure-intensive ablation technology, adjusted for development period and study requirements. The attributable input costs and earliest transaction records were not verified. This draft therefore explains the financing sequence and its limits without presenting a guessed requirement as observed fundraising.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

The original US brain indication followed the PMA route, P150038, approved on 11 July 2016. The FDA review describes a high-risk lesion-producing treatment, including preclinical/device testing, clinical evidence and manufacturing review. The clinical endpoint and patient selection belong to unilateral medication-refractory essential tremor. Later indications do not inherit identical evidence simply because the same platform is used. [@FDA-EXABLATE-P150038]

The relevant engineering safety case includes control of acoustic delivery and heating, image-based guidance, electrical/EMC behaviour and patient-contact materials. The review reports testing and a pre-approval manufacturing inspection. Its historical inspection conclusion is evidence about that approval process, not a complete current site list or independent audit of the present supply chain. The exact manufacturing location and outsourcing allocation were not established from the records used here. An Israeli company or R&D address alone would not prove where the finished system is manufactured. [@FDA-EXABLATE-P150038]

The standards story should remain linked to the actual risks and submission. Electrical/EMC and biological evaluation are documented categories; exact currently applicable editions and the complete conformity record still need verification. The current US quality framework also changed: QMSR amendments effective February 2026 incorporate ISO 13485:2016 requirements into Part 820. Older QS language should be identified as historical. [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

UK clinical-procedure guidance must be separated from device authorisation. NICE HTG733, published in December 2024, says more evidence is needed before NHS use of focused-ultrasound thalamotomy for moderate-to-severe Parkinsonian tremor and recommends use only in formal approved research. That is different from the essential-tremor commissioning route discussed below. It is also a procedure recommendation, not an MHRA registration or CE certificate. [@NICE-PD-HTG733]

Thus the report can describe original US market entry and an indication-specific UK adoption setting. It cannot claim a complete current global label, all later bilateral uses, or a verified present UK/EU device certificate from clinical service evidence alone.

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

NHS England's 2020 commissioning policy identifies a defined adult medication-refractory essential-tremor group unsuitable for DBS. This is a stronger payer starting point than a manufacturer assertion of UK availability. It should still be read as a specific policy with eligibility conditions, not a general entitlement for every tremor patient or Parkinson's indication. Current local arrangements and capacity require separate checking. [@NHSE-FOCUSED-ULTRASOUND-2020]

An England-specific economic model makes the value argument inspectable. In a five-year NHS-perspective model, Jameel and colleagues' body tables report total per-patient costs of £19,779 for MRgFUS, £62,348 for DBS and £3,735 for no procedure. The modelled MRgFUS/no-procedure base-case ICER is £20,851 per QALY. The abstract contains an inconsistent comparator-cost statement; the body tables are used here. These are historical modelled pathway costs, not current procurement quotes or observed savings. [@EXABLATE-ENGLAND-MODEL]

The economic interpretation is conditional. Relative value depends on clinical benefit, the comparator, time horizon and the way fixed equipment and treatment capacity are costed. A modelled advantage over DBS does not mean MRgFUS is cheaper than continued medical care, suitable for every DBS candidate or cash-saving in each hospital.

Published correspondence makes the uncertainty especially useful for a case study. Critics questioned throughput, capital-cost and comparator assumptions. The authors replied that their NHS reimbursement-based costing accounted for capital costs and discussed the scope of the comparison, explicitly identifying ExAblate 4000. Reading both sides prevents a criticism from becoming an unqualified allegation of error. [@EXABLATE-MODEL-EXCHANGE]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Selected patient] -->|referral and assessment| T[Specialist clinical team]
  T -->|treatment and follow-up| P
  I[Insightec] -->|system and support| H[Hospital service]
  H -->|procurement and capacity| I
  M[MRI facility and staff] -->|imaging and treatment resources| H
  T -->|selection and clinical requirements| H
  N[NHS commissioner] -.->|policy-eligible funded pathway| H
```

*Figure 1. Analytical map for an NHS essential-tremor service. The commissioning policy is documented; no specific equipment contract, local tariff or visit permission is asserted. Lecture-specific map formatting remains unavailable.*

The practical business question is how many appropriate patients a service can treat with its available scanner and specialist time. Fixed costs per case depend on usable capacity, while MRI time has an opportunity cost for other care. A current local costing exercise should identify equipment/service costs, treatment duration, staffing, failed eligibility screens and follow-up. It should not simply copy the model's total as the price of the machine.

The London connection is unusually relevant to these questions. The UCL/NHNN methods paper names ExAblate equipment, and the UCLH functional-neurosurgery service provides an enquiry route. That team could discuss patient selection, treatment workflow and local capacity within its experience. It is not automatically a source for original private financing or licence negotiations. No interview or observation visit has occurred. [@EXABLATE-LONDON] [@EXABLATE-UCLH] [@EXABLATE-SURGEON]

## Conclusion

Exablate provides the strongest UK service-and-payment story among these six drafts. Controlled original evidence, a defined commissioning policy, an England model and an exact-device London team make the pathway concrete. The case also shows why clinical novelty alone is insufficient: permanent-lesion risk, infrastructure, patient eligibility and throughput affect value. Earlier brain-specific finance, full first-version IP attribution and present manufacturing remain weaker.
