These gaps should be investigated directly, while keeping essential tremor separate from Parkinsonian tremor and distinguishing modelled pathway economics from actual procurement and payment.

reports.title: Turning spinal stimulation into a rehabilitation product
reports.scope: External ARC-EX for selected cervical SCI; implant/BCI programmes and home-use extension distinguished
reports.body_markdown:
## Executive summary

ONWARD Medical's ARC-EX is a case about turning external spinal stimulation into a rehabilitation product for selected people with cervical spinal cord injury. Its value depends on the combination of stimulation and purposeful training, rather than the stimulator alone. US regulatory records, the Up-LIFT study, academic/NRT disclosures and nearby UK providers support a substantial development and implementation narrative. [@FDA-ARCEX-DEN240014] [@ARCEX-UPLIFT]

The commercial account is less complete in two heavily weighted areas: exact original IP coverage and early product-specific finance. Payment is also unsettled in the reviewed evidence: a rehabilitation billing strategy or charity-supported device access is different from a verified routine payer commitment. ARC-EX is therefore attractive for first-hand investigation near London, while the current desk-based draft needs additional ownership, budget and transaction evidence.

## Device and case boundaries

ARC-EX uses skin electrodes connected to a programmable external stimulator, with software and professional control of treatment settings. It is used alongside rehabilitation to improve hand sensation and strength in the selected cervical-injury population. The proposed mechanism is to make surviving spinal circuitry more responsive during task practice. It does not read intentions from the brain, and its commercial lineage should be kept separate from ONWARD's implanted ARC-IM and BCI programmes. [@FDA-ARCEX-DEN240014] [@ARCEX-EU-IFU-REV5]

The original US authorisation concerns professional use; a later 510(k) extends use to the home under its conditions. Those settings have different staffing, training and payment implications. This report follows the external-device lineage and original market entry, then uses the home extension and UK provider experience to examine implementation.

## 1. Unmet medical need

The relevant problem is impaired upper-limb function after selected cervical spinal cord injuries, with consequences for independence and everyday tasks. Broad SCI burden establishes context but not product eligibility. A Spinal Injuries Association account of a 2024 NHS-data-based analysis reports about 105,000 people living with SCI in the UK and 4,400 new injuries/diagnoses each year. It includes traumatic and nontraumatic causes; the underlying linked-data analysis was not independently replicated here. [@ARCEX-UK-SCI-DATA]

This denominator differs from US traumatic-SCI statistics and is much broader than ARC-EX's original labelled/studied group. The US indication concerns ages 18–75 with chronic incomplete C2–C8 injury, subject to the full conditions. Injury level, completeness, chronicity, functional goals and suitability for training all matter. No reliable UK count meeting every criterion was identified. [@FDA-ARCEX-DEN240014]

Up-LIFT supplies the principal direct clinical evidence. It enrolled 65 participants; 60 completed the sequential programme of two months of rehabilitation alone followed by two months with stimulation added. Of the 60 completers, 43, or 71.7% (rounded to 72%), met the predefined combined strength-and-function responder endpoint. The safety population was 64, with no device-related serious adverse events reported. The study was prospective but single-arm and sequential, not randomised or sham-controlled. [@ARCEX-UPLIFT]

That design supports an encouraging clinical signal while leaving important causal questions. Continued practice, treatment order and expectations can contribute to change when every participant receives the same sequence. The 72% result is neither a response rate among every enrolled patient nor a guarantee that an unselected person with SCI benefits. It also should not be restated as universal neurological recovery.

The smaller UK Pathfinder2 study adds community-workflow evidence. Its abstract reports changes in selected functional measures but no significant group-level change in ISNCSCI motor/sensory scores. The distinction between functional task gains and broad neurological change is clinically and commercially important. The original records also disclose relevant provider/company interests, which should accompany interpretation of implementation claims. [@ARCEX-PATHFINDER] [@ARCEX-NEUROKINEX]

The unresolved economic need is to connect useful hand function with actual care consequences. Improved independence might affect assistance or participation, but no measured reduction in UK care expenditure caused by ARC-EX was verified. A model would need durable outcome data, training intensity, additional sessions, equipment costs and any change in care hours. High lifetime SCI costs alone cannot be treated as money this device will save.

## 2. Intellectual property

The external-stimulation origin has a documented academic/company relationship. Gerasimenko and colleagues' 2015 paper discloses Edgerton/Gerasimenko interests in NeuroRecovery Technologies (NRT), NRT's supply of the stimulator and inventor rights in UC Regents IP licensed to NRT/subsidiaries. The 2019 merger release and 2024 prospectus connect NRT and university licensing to the later company. These records support lineage, but do not supply the complete marketed ARC-EX licence schedule. [@ARCEX-EARLY-RESEARCH-LINEAGE] [@ARCEX-MERGER] [@ARCEX-PROSPECTUS]

The selected candidate patent, US10806927B2, names V. Reggie Edgerton, Yury Gerasimenko, Roland Roy and Daniel Lu, with priority from November 2011 and grant publication in October 2020. Its single independent claim was read in full for this draft. [@ARCEX-PATENT]

| Claim | Main content and attribution difficulty |
|---|---|
| 1 | Noninvasive transcutaneous stimulation over the brainstem/spinal cord enables voluntary control by making spinal circuitry receptive, rather than directly electrically inducing the function. The opening function list concerns postural/locomotor activity, leg-position movement and bladder voiding; a later clause also mentions stepping, standing, grasping and reaching. |

*Table 1. Independent claim 1 in US10806927B2. Its precise wording makes a direct mapping to the commercial hand-function indication uncertain. Related mechanism and shared inventors do not establish product coverage.* [@ARCEX-PATENT]

This is a consequential finding. It would be easy to cite the patent title and tell a broad story about all transcutaneous stimulation. Reading the claim exposes narrower combinations and wording that must be reconciled with the actual device. The present evidence does not justify calling this the definitive ARC-EX patent or assuming it appears in the licensed schedule.

The academic affiliations and licence disclosures also do not independently establish every inventor's employer at invention. University ownership, institutional laboratories and an individual's employment are distinct facts. Completing that chain requires original records or an attributable explanation. The case can describe an evidenced route from academic external stimulation through NRT into ONWARD while openly identifying the remaining claim-family and employment gaps.

## 3. Fundraising

Early academic support is identifiable. The 2015 predecessor paper acknowledges NIH awards U01EB15521 and R01EB007615, Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation support and other funders. The amounts are not supplied, and the research spans predecessor stimulation work rather than only the commercial hand-function device. Award identifiers are useful evidence of support and a route to further reconstruction; whole awards should not be allocated to ARC-EX without checking purpose and period. [@ARCEX-EARLY-RESEARCH-LINEAGE]

The corporate history contains a particularly important attribution trap. EPFL's 2016 announcement of €26 million equity plus a €10 million innovation loan explicitly concerns the implanted G-Therapeutics programme. It cannot be relabelled as €36 million of ARC-EX seed funding merely because the company lineage later joins. The 2024 prospectus separately records €5 million from former NRT investors in the merger context. That is more relevant to the external lineage, but still not the earliest NRT capital or a product-specific development budget. [@ARCEX-EARLYFIN] [@ARCEX-PROSPECTUS]

| Stage | Evidence | Correct allocation |
|---|---|---|
| Predecessor academic research | Named NIH/Reeve support | Research lineage; amounts and ARC-EX share unknown. |
| 2016 G-Therapeutics package | €26m equity + €10m loan | Implanted programme; excluded from an ARC-EX seed total. |
| 2019 merger context | Prospectus records €5m from former NRT investors | Combined-company/external-lineage context; not first-version spending. |
| UK study/access activity | Spinal Research/Neurokinex records | Later study or access support, not original invention capital. |

*Table 2. Financing evidence by programme and period. Currency is retained; no sum across rows is presented as historical ARC-EX R&D expenditure.* [@ARCEX-EARLYFIN] [@ARCEX-PROSPECTUS] [@ARCEX-NEUROKINEX] [@ARCEX-SPINALPROGRAM]

The entrepreneurial inference is that technology transfer and a corporate merger can combine different programmes and investors, making a current company's capital history a poor substitute for a device history. The report must follow the external technology through that transition, keeping implant funds and later access programmes separate.

Earliest commercial finance, valuation and attributable first-device expenditure remain unverified. A bottom-up reconstruction should include stimulator/control development, electrode integration, software, verification, rehabilitation-protocol development, trials, regulatory work and supplier setup through a defined authorisation milestone. A top-down comparison should match a noninvasive stimulation-plus-rehabilitation system. No adequately sourced unit costs or matched budgets were recovered, so a numerical funding requirement is not invented. This is one of the draft's largest remaining completeness gaps.

## 4. Regulatory route and manufacture

The original US De Novo authorisation, DEN240014, was issued on 19 December 2024. It establishes Class II classification under 21 CFR 890.5851, product code SDO. The later K251821 clearance, dated 14 November 2025, extends the use setting to the home under its label. That sequence is important: the first authorisation establishes the device type and controls, while later changes can use the resulting classification and predicate framework. [@FDA-ARCEX-DEN240014] [@FDA-ARCEX-K251821]

The FDA review addresses electrical/EMC safety, performance, software and skin-contact considerations. It cites standards including IEC 60601-1-2 and IEC 60601-2-10. Some biological evaluations rely on material history and previously cleared electrodes rather than new testing for every component. This is a more accurate description of the evidence strategy than implying that every item underwent an identical new test programme. [@FDA-ARCEX-DEN240014]

The product manual makes part of the supply chain concrete. The professional EU manual, Rev 5 issued 29 April 2026, identifies a Samsung tablet and Axelgaard PALS electrodes distributed by ONWARD. These specific component roles are stronger evidence than a supplier's general ability to design medical equipment. A historical prospectus description of enclosure development is a further design lead, but does not establish the current complete stimulator manufacturing chain. [@ARCEX-EU-IFU-REV5] [@ARCEX-PROSPECTUS]

ONWARD announced CE marking in September 2025, and its annual report states UK registration was completed. These are manufacturer records; the actual certificate and MHRA entry were not independently verified here. A manual, a provider listing or registration alone does not establish NHS commissioning. The US QMSR changes effective February 2026 supply current quality-system context, not a verified ONWARD compliance conclusion. [@ARCEX-CE] [@ARCEX-ANNUAL2025] [@FDA-QMSR-2026]

Home use adds a distinct implementation problem. The patient/helper must use a system whose settings and training remain professionally governed. That can extend access beyond a clinic, but also changes support, usability and financing requirements. The home clearance is therefore a new commercial setting, not proof that payment for the clinic model transfers automatically.

## 5. Reimbursement and stakeholder relationships

Three transactions need to be separated: financing a rehabilitation session, obtaining the stimulator and financing home use. ONWARD's 2025 annual report describes use of existing clinic rehabilitation billing routes while home-device benefit/category and coding work continued. That is the manufacturer's strategy, not an independent payer decision covering every ARC-EX component. [@ARCEX-ANNUAL2025]

UK access is more tangible than routine payment. Neurokinex explicitly describes ARC-EX alongside intensive activity-based rehabilitation, and the existing exact-device listings include Hemel Hempstead and Gatwick, outside London. Spinal Research's 2026 programme supports device loans to rehabilitation centres. A loan can lower a centre's access barrier, but does not establish how recurring sessions, staff, consumables and eventual equipment replacement are sustainably funded. [@ARCEX-NEUROKINEX-SERVICE] [@ARCEX-LOCATOR] [@ARCEX-SPINALPROGRAM]

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Selected patient and helper] -->|attendance and task practice| C[Rehabilitation centre]
  C -->|stimulation plus rehabilitation| P
  O[ONWARD] -->|system, software and training| C
  S[Spinal Research programme] -->|documented device-access support| C
  T[Therapists] -->|settings and outcome assessment| C
  Y[Patient, insurer or commissioner] -.->|terms require verification| C
  H[Home-use pathway] -.->|separate support and funding| P
```

*Figure 1. Analytical stakeholder map showing clinic, access-programme and home-use roles. The conditional payer/home arrows are questions, not verified contracts. The lecture-specific map format has not been supplied.*

An economic case should compare additional stimulation-related costs with durable functional benefit relative to the relevant rehabilitation alternative. If stimulation changes session length or training intensity, those costs belong in the comparison. If independence reduces care needs, the reduction must be measured rather than inferred from SCI burden. No verified ARC-EX-specific price, payer policy, routine NHS coverage or complete cost-effectiveness analysis was identified. Generic rehabilitation fees or charity programme prices are not valid substitutes for a device-specific episode price.

The nearby first-hand route is unusually useful for these gaps. The Neurokinex ARC-EX/Pathfinder2 team has a documented product relationship and can potentially discuss selection, session structure, training, outcomes and resource use. The London-based Spinal Research programme team can potentially explain study/access support and adoption barriers. Its office is not a treatment clinic. Provider/shareholder and company-author interests should be considered when interpreting accounts. No conversation, visit or patient access has been arranged. [@ARCEX-NEUROKINEX] [@ARCEX-PATHFINDER] [@ARCEX-SPINALCONTACT]

## Conclusion

ARC-EX provides a clinically interesting and locally investigable case about integrating a stimulation device with rehabilitation. The strongest evidence supports a defined original US indication, an encouraging but uncontrolled pivotal study, later home-use development and actual nearby service relationships. The most difficult parts are tracing exact original rights and finance through the academic/NRT/merger lineage, then demonstrating a sustainable payment model. A final report could improve substantially through targeted provider, funder and licensor evidence. Until then, strong trial and regulatory sections should not hide the weaker IP attribution, original-budget and payment evidence.

comparative_review_markdown:
# Comparing the six full report drafts

These are assessments of the **drafts and the evidence available to write them**, not rankings of clinical effectiveness or investment opportunities. Read the [six reports](README.md) alongside this review. No marks from a lecturer, independent examiner or predicted grade are claimed.

## Main finding

**RNS currently supports the most connected public case study. Exablate offers the strongest documented London investigation route and UK service/payment story. Ceribell is particularly useful for explaining academic technology transfer and early commercial finance.** SAINT has a coherent translation narrative but less complete present service economics. ARC-EX offers useful nearby exact-device access, while original IP/finance attribution and payment remain difficult. Precision has the greatest scope mismatch between an ambitious platform story and the evidence for the selected marketed component.

These differences emerged while writing the five sections, rather than from counting sources. The original quick access labels remain unchanged historical notes. This review assesses the new full drafts, including the additional research and deeper patent checks.

## How quality was judged

Project spec gives each content topic 17% and writing 15%. That makes a missing finance or reimbursement answer consequential even when the mechanism and trial sections are strong. I used the following questions, not an invented numerical score:

| Area | What a good draft should do |
|---|---|
| Unmet need | Define the original patient problem; quantify a scoped population and geography; compare prior care, outcomes and costs without equating burden with device benefit. |
| IP | Trace the first invention and inventors/employers; explain the selected independent claims; distinguish technical candidates, actual licensed rights and exact product coverage. |
| Fundraising | Give dated early sources/amounts and valuations where available; distinguish company capital, device expenditure, grants, debt/conversion and later growth. If estimating required capital, provide justified inputs and a method. |
| Regulatory/manufacturing | Explain the original market route and supporting evidence, relevant standards and actual manufacturing responsibilities; retain version and country boundaries. |
| Reimbursement | Identify the payer/buyer and payment conditions, distinguish codes/coverage/amounts from models, and analyse the whole pathway with a stakeholder map. |
| Writing | Lead with a case-specific conclusion, develop a coherent argument, use clear paragraphs and informative captions, keep citations retrievable and remain within the word budget. |

The source guide and the Optomed/Quadsense audit informed the use of broader sources. Those examples do not prove that every source or inference would receive lecturer approval. The separate [writing-method note](../docs/full-report-writing-method.md) records the actual module materials used and the limits of review.

## Where the five sections stand

| Draft | Unmet need | IP | Fundraising | Regulatory/manufacture | Reimbursement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [RNS](../devices/rns/full-report.md) | Randomised and long-term evidence; eligible population and UK costs incomplete | Both foundational independent claims explained; employment/assignment and current coverage incomplete | Pre-approval offering quantified; earliest finance and valuation incomplete | Original PMA, model-specific MRI and dated manufacturing disclosure | Actual payer criteria plus a nine-year model; fees and NHS access incomplete |
| [Ceribell](../devices/ceribell/full-report.md) | Strong access/workflow narrative; patient-outcome and realised-savings evidence weaker | All four selected independent claims plus actual Stanford licence terms; later AI mapping incomplete | Academic seed and early company proceeds traced; grant value and valuations missing | Hardware/software generations and dated sourcing distinguished; complete current standards/markets incomplete | Device-specific model and NTAP update; current commercial terms and post-add-on economics unresolved |
| [Exablate](../devices/exablate/full-report.md) | Controlled trial and a defined treatment pathway; current eligible volumes incomplete | Four independent claims explained in a relevant candidate family; exact original product attribution incomplete | Agreement/closing sequence recovered; valuation conflict and brain-only budget unresolved | Original PMA and indication-specific UK guidance; manufacturing detail incomplete | NHS policy, England model and critique/reply; local price/capacity inputs incomplete |
| [SAINT](../devices/saint/full-report.md) | Direct small trial and UK comparator context; durability, local population and costs incomplete | Four independent claims and licensor evidence; full product/rights map incomplete | Named academic support and $25m launch round; early allocation/valuation missing | Defined cleared system, standards and a named supplier; complete current UK/EU status incomplete | Temporary inpatient support updated; current package economics and coverage incomplete |
| [ARC-EX](../devices/arcex/full-report.md) | Defined indication and pivotal/community studies; causal and care-cost limits visible | Full selected independent claim read, exposing a product-scope mismatch | Academic support and merger context; earliest external-device capital unverified | De Novo/home sequence and actual component suppliers; certificate/current full chain incomplete | Real provider/charity access; no verified specific fee, coverage or complete economic model |
| [Precision](../devices/precision/full-report.md) | Clear component boundary and acute feasibility; eligible market and comparative value missing | Four application claims explained; marketed-component mapping and later legal position incomplete | Early rounds traced; component budget/valuation missing | Specific clearance, testing and foundry acquisition; current complete supply chain incomplete | Official system context only; no exact component payment or procurement record |

This table intentionally gives the reason for each assessment. “Many papers” or a polished narrative would not answer the missing questions.

## Assessment of each draft and actual writing difficulties

### RNS: the most complete account for public desk research

The draft can connect an original patient group, controlled evidence, longer follow-up, a foundational architecture, pre-approval capital, manufacturing and a payer policy. This makes its central argument easier to sustain across the whole report. The economic model and payer policy also let the reimbursement section explain value and eligibility separately.

The difficult part was preserving time and scope. The 75% nine-year reduction is open-label follow-up, whereas the earlier 37.9%/17.3% figures belong to the blinded trial. The 2011 filing reports securities sold, not a completed all-cash round. MRI status differs by model. Treating any of these as a single universal product fact would have produced a smoother but less reliable story.

The draft still lacks the first funding/employment/assignment chain, actual current fees and a verified NHS pathway. It is the strongest starting draft, not a completed submission. A useful next investigation would target the earliest company history rather than add another recent clinical paper.

### Ceribell: strongest academic-to-company detail, harder outcome economics

The combination of an actual university licence, grant attribution, early net proceeds and original hardware decisions gives this draft unusually specific development material. The report can explain how a clinical access problem became a licensed, manufactured product without relying only on company slogans.

The hardest writing task was separating at least three things: the original rapid-EEG hardware/sonification, later automated software and newer payment decisions. DECIDE measures access and physician decisions; it is not an AI accuracy trial or mortality trial. A 38-patient pilot with one positive case cannot support an impressive-looking perfect-sensitivity claim. The economic paper predicts savings, and the expired seizure-monitor add-on cannot be replaced by citing a separate delirium award.

The present draft is strong on origin, finance and version history. Its weaker part is demonstrating realised patient/cost benefit and sustainable current purchasing/payment terms. A hospital workflow and finance discussion would add more than another founder biography.

### Exablate: strongest opportunity to improve the draft through London investigation

This draft has the clearest connection among actual local equipment, a specialist team, an NHS commissioning source and an England economic model. It can discuss how infrastructure and patient selection affect an established service, and the model's published critique/reply supports real critical analysis.

The difficult part was preventing apparent contradictions from being silently resolved. The 2012 agreement and closing differ; one document also contains conflicting valuation figures. The economic abstract has a comparator-cost inconsistency, so the body tables were used. A critique questioned cost assumptions, but the authors' reply needed to be read before claiming an omission. Essential-tremor and Parkinsonian-tremor NHS positions also differ.

The draft is convincing on the service/value question, but exact first-version IP, early brain-specific capital and manufacture remain underdeveloped. The London team is a useful route for patient selection and capacity, not automatically for confidential company finance. If firsthand investigation is a priority, this is the most promising report to take forward.

### SAINT: coherent translation story, incomplete ongoing business model

The draft has a clear central question: whether a personalised five-day treatment can be delivered reproducibly and paid for sustainably. The academic/licensor, launch-finance, clearance and supplier records support that question well.

Writing was difficult because dramatic remission percentages can dominate the story. The early trial is small and stopped at an interim analysis; the original regulatory tables also have an inconsistent active/sham header. The draft follows the consistent narrative/rows and retains the denominator. A four-to-six-week UK comparator is useful service context but not SAINT evidence. Fifty sessions and 500 active stimulation minutes also show why a compressed calendar does not establish low resource use.

The weakest section is present service economics after the inpatient NTAP ends. Durability, retreatment, MRI/staff inputs and actual current coverage require better evidence. A London TMS clinic should only be used for a clearly scoped comparator/workflow question unless licensed SAINT delivery is verified.

### ARC-EX: strong implementation potential, significant historical attribution gaps

The clinical/regulatory narrative is substantial, and the nearby provider/funder relationships give a realistic way to ask practical questions. This draft is useful for understanding a device whose performance depends on rehabilitation delivery as much as equipment.

The largest difficulty was following the external technology through academic work, NRT, a merger and a company with distinct implanted programmes. The €36m G-Therapeutics package is explicitly implant-related and cannot be assigned to ARC-EX. The candidate patent's independent claim has a function-scope complication for hand-function attribution. The 72% trial result uses 60 completers, not all 65 enrolled, and the sequential design does not remove training/order effects.

The report reads coherently but remains materially incomplete in original IP, earliest product finance and payment. Charity loans and a provider listing do not settle sustainable reimbursement. Provider/funder conversations could improve implementation and payment evidence; a licensor/company history source is needed for the original rights and capital questions.

### Precision: hardest to complete without choosing a much narrower question

The draft's main strength is a disciplined boundary around the marketed temporary Layer 7-T. Early rounds, a fabrication acquisition, technical evidence and a relevant application claim set provide a useful staged-development case.

The hardest writing problem is that the most compelling platform narrative concerns a future assistive BCI, while the selected clearance concerns a temporary electrode. Paralysis burden, secondary-device control claims and future home-use economics cannot automatically justify the current component's market. Acute feasibility also does not establish a comparative clinical benefit or a procurement case.

The draft therefore has the largest unresolved connection between need, benefit and payment. A product-specific clinical/purchasing source and eligible procedure count would change its quality more than broader neurotechnology coverage. It is a valid entrepreneurship case, but currently the hardest one to finish convincingly across all five weighted topics.

## What remains incomplete in all six drafts

Each draft contains all five narrative sections, a description, claim analysis, financing discussion, an analytical stakeholder diagram, conclusion and retrievable references. Each is within the 4,000-word budget under the recorded counting method. This is structural completion, not a declaration that every specification question is answered.

No original interviews were conducted. Contemporaneous inventor employment and exact product-to-claim maps remain incomplete. No fully justified bottom-up/top-down numerical estimate of missing early capital was produced because attributable staff, study and manufacturing costs were not verified; the drafts explain the method and missing inputs instead of presenting invented history. That is a real funding weakness against the specification, not something a longer paragraph solves.

Current local prices, full current multi-market authorisation and independently verified manufacturing chains are uneven. The stakeholder diagrams are analytical drafts because the lecture-specific required format was not supplied. The documents do not include invented group responsibilities or a false AI-policy declaration, and should not be treated as assessed submissions.

## Practical choice for the team

For a public-source project with the fewest disconnected sections, **start with RNS**. For a London investigation that could materially improve service, cost and adoption analysis, **start with Exablate**. For a strong academic licensing and early-finance story, **consider Ceribell**. ARC-EX remains attractive if the team values its mechanism and can pursue the specific provider/funder/licensor gaps. SAINT is coherent but needs a firmer service-economics account; Precision requires the clearest scope decision and the most original procurement/eligible-market work.

These recommendations concern research feasibility and draft completeness. They are not clinical recommendations or evidence that one technology is medically better than another.
writing_method_markdown:
# How the full drafts were written

## Reader and purpose

The reader is an Imperial engineering teammate familiar with the entrepreneurship module, but not necessarily with the selected clinical condition. Each draft asks how a defined device moved from an unmet need through invention, capital and regulation into a deliverable and fundable clinical pathway. This is a set of AI-generated reference drafts for comparison and discussion, not an assessed submission or a compliance declaration.

## Course materials actually used

| Material | Guidance applied | Review boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Project spec 2026, pp1–3 | Early device development; five content topics; quantitative who/what/when/how much; 17% per topic and 15% writing; whole-document 4,000-word limit; retrievable references; informative captions | All three pages had previously been extracted and visually checked; the complete extracted text was reread for these drafts. |
| Optomed Aurora example | Combine disease/care-pathway sources with product evidence; distinguish assumptions; make references retrievable without hidden hyperlinks | Used the existing page/reference audit and observed reference-loss warning; not treated as blanket source endorsement. |
| Quadsense example | Explain technical claims, financing and stakeholder relationships; avoid basic module explanations and unsupported paraphrase | Used the audited sections and visible feedback. Reported interviews belong to the original authors, not this team. |
| Nature, The write stuff | Lead with a central message and maintain one argument through the case | Selected downloaded text and the workspace writing guide reviewed; writing advice is not clinical evidence. |
| Savage and Yeh/Cormac McCarthy writing advice | Concrete sentences, one point per paragraph, remove repetition | Applied as editorial guidance, not a course requirement. |
| Write to Express, Not to Impress | Prefer plain words and active, direct explanations | Selected downloaded text reread; examples were not copied. |
| Humphrey and Holmes communication book | Outline, paragraph continuity, citation and critical editing | Used previously reviewed selected passages and the retained writing guide; the complete book was not reread. |
| Five Steps to Create Meaningful, Visual Reports | Give each table/diagram a real explanatory role | Applied to claim/finance tables and stakeholder diagrams; no decorative performance score. |
| Company-information resource handout | Mine filings and distinguish responsible-party records from leads | Used through the specification/source-guide workflow; existing investor/funder/filing evidence carried forward. |
| Vocabulary link resources | Keep grant, equity, loan, conversion, valuation, payer and buyer distinct | Saved link pages are not complete archived external glossaries; no unreviewed glossary content is attributed. |

The Jeff Fredburg PDF contains a YouTube link only. Its lecture was not transcribed or watched for this task, so no lecture-specific advice is claimed. Original course/example PDFs remain outside the public repository.

## Structure and evidence handling

Each draft leads with its main case-study conclusion, defines the product and original market endpoint, then develops unmet need, IP, fundraising, regulation/manufacture and reimbursement. Device-specific terms are introduced where necessary; generic explanations of patents and venture capital are omitted because the reader is assumed to know the module.

The [reliability protocol](reliability-protocol.md) governs claims. Direct records, context, model results and our analysis remain distinguishable in the prose. The original two research layers are retained separately. All 19 independent claims in the six selected patent publications were read for drafting; this completes that selected-publication reading, not a complete product/portfolio or legal analysis. The ARC-EX claim wording exposes a significant product-attribution uncertainty.

Deeper checks also read the RNS economic paper's publisher abstract, its 2021 prospectus manufacturing passages, Ceribell's DECIDE study and economic-model passages, selected original FDA sections/standards and current government quality-system context. Review coverage is recorded in data/full-report-evidence.json. Inaccessible publisher pages were not treated as fully reviewed; regulator summaries or actually retrieved text were used within their scope.

References are numbered at first appearance and include source identity, date where known, stable public URL and review date. No personal communication is cited. Plain URLs remain visible in the reference list so exported text retains the retrieval route. Body citations do not depend on embedded hyperlinks.

Each stakeholder diagram is labelled as an analytical draft. Solid arrows show stated roles; conditional payer arrows are explicit. It does not document every contract or replace the unavailable lecture format. No interview, clinical visit or outreach has occurred.

## Limits and quality checks

Missing data were not filled with plausible-sounding figures. In particular, no device budget was inferred from total company capital, no model result was presented as observed savings and no general provider fee was used as a device price. Where earliest finance remains missing, the drafts explain bottom-up/top-down reconstruction and required inputs; they do not pretend this substitutes for a justified numerical estimate. The [comparative review](../reports/comparative-review.md) treats that as a weakness.

Validation checks six-device/five-topic scope, citation resolution, retrievable references, word budgets, selected claim coverage and preservation of the earlier research records. Counts use whitespace-separated tokens in the entire Markdown file, including references, tables, diagrams and notices. This conservative working count is not guaranteed to match Word or Turnitin; the drafts retain a margin below 4,000. Structural checks are not independent semantic verification.

The comparison is a qualitative self-audit of these drafts against the specification. It reports strengths, incomplete answers and writing difficulties. It predicts neither lecturer marks nor clinical superiority, and source counts do not determine quality.
